html:
Nuclear physics is the heaviest chapter of Modern Physics: the area carries 12 of the 50 Physics questions, and we estimate about 3 come from here — more than any other modern topic.

The paper asks for the size and density of a nucleus, a mass defect or binding-energy calculation, the difference between fission and fusion, the three radiations, and — above all — the half-life.

The half-life questions are the easiest marks in the chapter if you count in halves rather than reach for the exponential, and the easiest to lose if you forget that a half-life does not change with temperature, pressure or chemical combination.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • R = R_0A^{1/3} with R_0 \approx 1.2 fm, and why nuclear density is the same for every nucleus.
  • Mass defect, \Delta E = \Delta m\,c^2, and the conversion 1 u = 931.5 MeV.
  • The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve: peak at iron, fission of heavy nuclei, fusion of light nuclei.
  • Fission and fusion, one example of each, and why each releases energy.
  • Alpha, beta and gamma: charge, mass, penetration, ionising power, deflection in a field.
  • N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}, T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda, \tau = 1/\lambda, activity A = \lambda N.
  • Carbon dating as a half-life calculation.
  • Medical uses (diagnosis vs therapy) and the hazards of ionising radiation.

20.1 The nucleus: charge, size, mass and density; mass defect, binding energy and E = mc²

What is inside the nucleus

A nucleus of element X is written ^{A}_{Z}X, where Z is the atomic number (the number of protons) and A the mass number (protons + neutrons). The neutrons number N = A - Z. Protons and neutrons together are nucleons.

Property Value or rule
Charge +Ze; the electron cloud carries -Ze, so the atom is neutral
Radius R = R_0A^{1/3}, R_0 \approx 1.2 fm (1\ \text{fm} = 10^{-15} m)
Volume \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3A \propto A
Density \rho = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3} \approx 2.3\times10^{17} kg m⁻³
Mass of proton 1.007276 u = 938.3 MeV/c^2
Mass of neutron 1.008665 u = 939.6 MeV/c^2
Mass of electron 0.000549 u = 0.511 MeV/c^2

The key point about the radius formula is the cube root. If A becomes eight times larger, the radius only doubles.

So the volume is proportional to A, and the density is the same for every nucleus — about 2.3\times10^{17} kg m⁻³, some 10^{14} times the density of water. A teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh about a billion tonnes.

Radius, not diameter

The formula gives the radius. A question that asks for the diameter wants 2R_0A^{1/3}. And R_0 is about 1.2 fm; if a question gives 1.1 or 1.3 fm, use the value given.

Worked example 20.1 — the size of a uranium nucleus

Problem. Find the radius and density of a ^{238}U nucleus (R_0 = 1.2 fm).

Solution. A^{1/3} = 238^{1/3} = 6.20, so R = 1.2\times6.20 = 7.4 fm. Density \rho = \dfrac{3(1.66\times10^{-27})}{4\pi(1.2\times10^{-15})^3} = 2.3\times10^{17} kg m⁻³. The same answer comes from any nucleus — that is the point of R \propto A^{1/3}.

Mass defect and binding energy

A nucleus weighs less than the sum of its separate protons and neutrons. The missing mass is the mass defect:

\Delta m = \left[Zm_p + (A-Z)m_n\right] - M_{nucleus}

The missing mass has become binding energy, the energy that would be needed to pull the nucleus apart:

E_b = \Delta m\,c^2

This is Einstein's mass–energy relation E = mc^2 applied to the nucleus: mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, related by the square of the speed of light. A mass of 1 u corresponds to

1\ \text{u} \times c^2 = 931.5\ \text{MeV}

so the practical rule is energy in MeV = mass defect in u × 931.5.

When atomic masses are used instead of nuclear masses, the electron masses cancel if you use the mass of the hydrogen atom in place of the proton:

\Delta m = Zm_H + (A-Z)m_n - M_{atom}

Binding energy of a helium nucleus

Setting up. A ^4He nucleus has 2 protons and 2 neutrons. m_H = 1.007825 u, m_n = 1.008665 u, and the atomic mass of ^4He is 4.002603 u.

Step 1 — mass of the separate parts. 2(1.007825) + 2(1.008665) = 2.015650 + 2.017330 = 4.032980 u.

Step 2 — mass defect. \Delta m = 4.032980 - 4.002603 = 0.030377 u.

Step 3 — convert to energy. E_b = 0.030377 \times 931.5 = 28.3 MeV.

Step 4 — per nucleon. 28.3/4 = 7.07 MeV per nucleon.

What it means. Each nucleon in helium is bound by about 7 MeV, which is why helium is unusually stable for such a light nucleus.

The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve

Plot E_b/A against A and you get the most important graph in nuclear physics.

  • It rises steeply for the lightest nuclei: deuterium 1.1, helium-4 7.07, carbon-12 7.68, oxygen-16 7.98 MeV per nucleon.
  • It reaches a broad maximum of about 8.8 MeV near iron-56 (and nickel-62 is marginally higher — the difference is small and not examinable).
  • It then falls slowly for heavy nuclei: lead about 7.9, uranium-238 about 7.6.

Why the curve matters. A system tends towards the lowest energy, which means the highest binding energy per nucleon. Any change that moves a nucleus up the curve releases energy.

  • Fusion of light nuclei (moving towards the peak) releases energy — the Sun runs this way.
  • Fission of heavy nuclei (splitting into two mid-mass fragments nearer the peak) releases energy — reactors and bombs run this way.
  • Iron is the end of the road. You cannot get energy by fusing iron into heavier nuclei, because that moves down the curve. This is why massive stars develop iron cores and then collapse.
Binding energy is not "energy stored in the nucleus"

A high binding energy means the nucleus is hard to break apart, so it is stable. The energy is released when the nucleus forms, not stored for later use.

When students say "the nucleus contains 28 MeV of binding energy", they mean the nucleus is bound by 28 MeV relative to its separated nucleons.

20.2 Nuclear fission and fusion

Fission

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two medium-mass nuclei, with the release of two or three neutrons and about 200 MeV of energy.

A typical reaction:

^{235}_{92}\text{U} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow\ ^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + ^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3\,^{1}_{0}\text{n} + 200\ \text{MeV}

Check the bookkeeping: mass numbers 235 + 1 = 141 + 92 + 3 = 236; charges 92 = 56 + 36. Both are conserved.

The energy appears because the fragments have higher binding energy per nucleon (about 8.5 MeV) than uranium-238 (7.6 MeV). The mass lost is about 0.2 u per fission, which is 0.2 \times 931.5 \approx 200 MeV.

Chain reaction. Each fission releases 2–3 neutrons, which can trigger further fissions. If on average more than one neutron succeeds, the reaction is self-sustaining. The minimum mass needed to sustain it is the critical mass; below it too many neutrons escape.

Reactor part Job Material
Fuel provides fissile nuclei enriched uranium (U-235)
Moderator slows neutrons so they are captured more easily heavy water, graphite, ordinary water
Control rods absorb neutrons and hold the rate steady boron, cadmium
Coolant carries heat to the turbine water, CO₂
Shield absorbs radiation thick concrete

Fusion

Nuclear fusion is the joining of light nuclei into a heavier one, with the release of energy. It is the source of the Sun's energy.

^{2}_{1}\text{H} + ^{3}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow\ ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} + 17.6\ \text{MeV}

In the Sun the proton–proton chain combines four protons into one helium nucleus, with two positrons and two neutrinos:

4\,^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow\ ^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2e^{+} + 2\nu + 26.7\ \text{MeV}

Why fusion needs a very high temperature. Both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel each other.

To get close enough for the short-range strong force to act, they must approach at high speed — which means a temperature of the order of 10^7 K. This is the Coulomb barrier, and it is why fusion is hard to sustain on Earth.

Fission Fusion
What happens heavy nucleus splits light nuclei join
Fuel uranium-235, plutonium-239 deuterium, tritium
Energy per event about 200 MeV about 17.6 MeV (D–T)
Energy per nucleon about 0.85 MeV about 3.5 MeV
Needs a critical mass and a neutron extremely high temperature
Where reactors, weapons stars; experimental reactors
Which way does the energy go?

Fission releases energy because the fragments are more tightly bound than the parent. Fusion releases energy because the product is more tightly bound than the reactants. Both are "moving up the curve". Fusing nuclei heavier than iron absorbs energy instead.

20.3 Radioactivity: alpha, beta and gamma rays; the decay law, half-life and mean life; carbon dating

The three radiations

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus. It was discovered by Becquerel in 1896 and studied by Marie and Pierre Curie.

It is a nuclear process: it does not depend on temperature, pressure or chemical combination, because the energy involved is millions of times larger than chemical energies.

Property Alpha (\alpha) Beta (\beta^-) Gamma (\gamma)
Nature helium nucleus ^{4}_{2}He electron e^- photon
Charge +2e -e 0
Mass 4 u \approx 1/1836 u 0
Speed \sim 0.05c up to \sim 0.99c c
Ionising power very strong moderate weak
Penetration a few cm of air, stopped by paper a few mm of aluminium needs cm of lead or concrete
Deflection in an electric field towards the negative plate towards the positive plate none
Effect on nucleus A falls by 4, Z falls by 2 Z rises by 1 (for \beta^-) no change

Alpha decay reduces both A and Z:

^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow\ ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}

Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton inside the nucleus:

^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow\ ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + e^- + \bar\nu_e

A is unchanged and Z rises by one. The emitted electron is created at the moment of decay — it was not orbiting the nucleus.

Beta-plus decay converts a proton into a neutron, emitting a positron:

^{22}_{11}\text{Na} \rightarrow\ ^{22}_{10}\text{Ne} + e^+ + \nu_e

Gamma emission is a photon emitted when an excited daughter nucleus drops to a lower energy state. It changes neither A nor Z.

Where the beta electron comes from

Students often say "the nucleus contains electrons". It does not. In \beta^- decay a neutron turns into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino: n \to p + e^- + \bar\nu_e. The electron is born in the decay.

The continuous beta energy spectrum (the electron rarely gets the full available energy) was the evidence that a second particle, the neutrino, carries the rest.

The decay law

Radioactive decay is random: we cannot say when a particular nucleus will decay, only the probability per unit time, \lambda, the decay constant. For N nuclei,

\frac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}

The activity A is the number of decays per second:

A = \lambda N = A_0e^{-\lambda t}

Its SI unit is the becquerel (Bq), one decay per second. The older unit, the curie (Ci), is 3.7\times10^{10} Bq — roughly the activity of 1 g of radium-226.

Half-life and mean life

The half-life T_{1/2} is the time for half of the nuclei (or half the activity) to decay. Putting N = N_0/2 in the decay law:

\frac{1}{2} = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}

The mean life \tau is the average lifetime of a nucleus:

\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{T_{1/2}}{\ln 2} = 1.44\,T_{1/2}

After n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)^n:

Half-lives elapsed Fraction remaining Fraction decayed
0 1 0
1 1/2 1/2
2 1/4 3/4
3 1/8 7/8
4 1/16 15/16
n 2^{-n} 1 - 2^{-n}

Half-life is a nuclear property

T_{1/2} does not change with temperature, pressure, chemical state, or whether the element is free or in a compound. Chemical reactions involve electron energies of a few eV; nuclear decay involves MeV. Heating a radium salt does not make it decay faster.

Worked example 20.2 — counting in halves

Problem. A sample has an activity of 6400 Bq and a half-life of 5 days. What is its activity after 20 days?

Solution. 20/5 = 4 half-lives. Activity = 6400/2^4 = 6400/16 = 400 Bq. No logarithms needed — count the halvings.

Worked example 20.3 — from activity to half-life

Problem. A source contains 4.0\times10^{15} nuclei and has an activity of 2.0\times10^{8} Bq. Find the decay constant and the half-life.

Solution. \lambda = A/N = 2.0\times10^8/4.0\times10^{15} = 5.0\times10^{-8} s⁻¹. T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda = 1.4\times10^7 s \approx 160 days.

Carbon dating

Carbon-14 is produced in the upper atmosphere when cosmic-ray neutrons strike nitrogen-14:

^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow\ ^{14}_{6}\text{C} + ^{1}_{1}\text{H}

Living things take in carbon continuously, so the ratio of ^{14}C to ^{12}C in their tissue stays at the atmospheric value (about 1 part in 10^{12}).

When the organism dies, intake stops and the ^{14}C decays with a half-life of 5730 years. Measuring the remaining activity gives the time since death.

Worked example 20.4 — dating a bone

Problem. A bone sample has 25 % of the ^{14}C activity of living tissue. How old is it? (T_{1/2} = 5730 yr)

Solution. 25\% = 1/4 = (1/2)^2, so two half-lives have passed: t = 2\times5730 = 11{,}460 years.

The method works up to about 50,000 years (about nine half-lives), beyond which the remaining activity is too small to measure reliably.

It also assumes the atmospheric ^{14}C ratio has stayed constant; calibration with tree rings and other methods corrects for the small variations.

Parent–daughter chains

A radioactive nucleus usually decays into another radioactive nucleus, and so on, until a stable one is reached. These are the decay series:

Series Parent Stable end Half-life of parent
Uranium ^{238}U ^{206}Pb 4.5\times10^9 yr
Thorium ^{232}Th ^{208}Pb 1.4\times10^{10} yr
Actinium ^{235}U ^{207}Pb 7.0\times10^8 yr

If the parent has N_0 nuclei at t = 0 and the daughter is stable, the number of daughter nuclei at time t is the number that have decayed:

N_d = N_0\left(1 - e^{-\lambda t}\right)

At t = T_{1/2} half the parent has become daughter; as t \to \infty all of it does. In a long chain the slowest step controls the overall rate, and after enough time the whole chain reaches secular equilibrium, in which every member decays at the same activity.

20.4 Medical uses of nuclear radiation and its health hazards

Diagnosis

Diagnosis uses small doses to see inside the body. The radiation must be penetrating enough to escape and be detected outside.

Technique Radiation What it shows
X-ray radiograph X-rays bones, lungs, dental work
CT scan X-rays from many angles cross-sectional images
Bone scan ^{99m}Tc (γ, T_{1/2} 6 h) bone tumours, fractures
PET scan ^{18}F in glucose (β⁺, T_{1/2} 110 min) metabolic activity, cancer
Thyroid scan ^{131}I (γ and β) thyroid function

A tracer should be a gamma emitter with a short half-life: gamma rays escape the body, and a short half-life keeps the dose low.

Alpha emitters are a poor choice for tracers because alpha particles are stopped inside the body and deposit all their energy in a small volume.

Therapy

Therapy uses large doses to destroy tissue — usually a tumour.

  • External radiotherapy: a beam of gamma rays from cobalt-60 is aimed at the tumour from several directions, so the tumour receives a high dose while each patch of healthy skin receives less.
  • Brachytherapy: a sealed source is placed inside or next to the tumour.
  • Targeted therapy: radioactive iodine-131 is taken up by thyroid cells, so it irradiates the thyroid from inside — useful for hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer.

The difference between diagnosis and therapy is dose and intent: the same isotope can do both, but at very different activities.

Hazards

Ionising radiation damages cells by breaking chemical bonds, especially in DNA.

Effect When Examples
Somatic (in the exposed person) soon after a large dose skin burns, nausea, hair loss, radiation sickness
Long-term somatic years later leukaemia, thyroid and lung cancer, cataracts
Genetic in the next generation mutations in germ cells

Dose units. The gray (Gy) is the absorbed energy per unit mass (1 Gy = 1 J kg⁻¹). The sievert (Sv) is the equivalent dose, which allows for the fact that alpha particles do more biological damage per joule than gamma rays.

Natural background radiation gives about 2–3 mSv per year.

Protection. Three rules:

  1. Time — spend as little time near the source as possible.
  2. Distance — dose falls as 1/r^2, so doubling the distance quarters it.
  3. Shielding — lead for gamma, plastic or paper for beta, and never alpha emitters inside the body.

Workers wear film badges or electronic dosimeters, and hospitals follow the ALARA principle: doses as low as reasonably achievable.

The danger is not "radioactivity" in general

A smoke detector contains a tiny americium-241 source and is safe because the alpha particles cannot escape the casing. A diagnostic tracer is safe because the activity is small and the half-life short.

The hazard comes from dose, not from the mere presence of a radioactive atom.

Formula and fact sheet

Quantity Formula or value
Nuclear radius R = R_0A^{1/3}, R_0 \approx 1.2 fm
Nuclear density \rho \approx 2.3\times10^{17} kg m⁻³, independent of A
Mass defect \Delta m = Zm_H + (A-Z)m_n - M_{atom}
Binding energy E_b = \Delta m\,c^2; 1 u = 931.5 MeV
BE per nucleon maximum 8.8 MeV near Fe-56
Fission ^{235}U + n → Ba + Kr + 3n + 200 MeV
Fusion ^{2}H + ^{3}H → ^{4}He + n + 17.6 MeV
Sun's chain 4 ^{1}H → ^{4}He + 2e⁺ + 2ν + 26.7 MeV
Alpha decay A \to A-4, Z \to Z-2
Beta-minus A same, Z \to Z+1; n \to p + e^- + \bar\nu
Beta-plus A same, Z \to Z-1; p \to n + e^+ + \nu
Gamma A and Z unchanged
Decay law N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}; A = \lambda N
Half-life T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda
Mean life \tau = 1/\lambda = 1.44\,T_{1/2}
After n half-lives N = N_0/2^n

Carbon-14 T_{1/2} = 5730 yr; useful to ~50,000 yr

Background about 2–3 mSv per year

Chapter summary

  • The nucleus has Z protons and A-Z neutrons; R = R_0A^{1/3}, so volume \propto A and density is the same for all nuclei (2.3\times10^{17} kg m⁻³).
  • A nucleus is lighter than its parts by \Delta m; the missing mass is the binding energy, E_b = \Delta m c^2, with 1 u = 931.5 MeV.
  • Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56 at 8.8 MeV. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move nuclei up this curve and release energy.
  • Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into two mid-mass fragments plus neutrons, releasing about 200 MeV; a chain reaction needs a critical mass.
  • Fusion: light nuclei join, releasing energy; it needs about 10^7 K to overcome the Coulomb barrier, and powers the Sun.
  • Alpha is a helium nucleus (A-4, Z-2), beta is an electron or positron (Z\pm1), gamma is a photon (no change). Alpha ionises most and penetrates least; gamma is the reverse.
  • N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}, T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda, \tau = 1/\lambda; after n half-lives a fraction 2^{-n} remains. Half-life is unaffected by temperature or chemical state.
  • Activity A = \lambda N, measured in becquerels; 1 Ci = 3.7\times10^{10} Bq.
  • Carbon dating uses the 5730-year half-life of carbon-14; 25 % activity means two half-lives, about 11,460 years.
  • Diagnosis uses small doses of gamma emitters; therapy uses large doses to kill cells. Hazards are somatic and genetic; protection is time, distance and shielding.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (d) — R = R_0A^{1/3}: volume ∝ A at constant density.

2. (a) — 1\ \mathrm{u} \times c^2 = 931.5 MeV; (d) 0.511 MeV is the electron's rest energy.

3. (c) — the vanished mass is the binding energy, E = \Delta m c^2.

4. (b) — ≈ 8.8 MeV per nucleon near Fe-56/Ni-62.

5. (a) — the α carries away 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

6. (d) — a neutron becomes a proton: Z + 1, A unchanged.

7. (b) — exponential decay: each nucleus has the same decay probability per second, λ.

8. (c) — T_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambda.

9. (b) — \tau = 1/\lambda = T_{1/2}/0.693 = 1.44\,T_{1/2}.

10. (a) — 1 Bq = 1 decay per second; the curie (3.7\times10^{10} Bq) is the older unit.

11. (d) — C-14, replenished by cosmic rays in life, decaying after death.

12. (c) — slow (thermal) neutrons fission U-235 best; rods (b-option confusion) absorb.

13. (a) — about 200 MeV, mostly the fragments' KE.

14. (c) — the proton–proton chain fusing H into He at 1.5\times10^7 K in the core.

15. (b) — high-energy photons emitted by de-exciting nuclei.

16. (d) — α, massive and doubly charged, spends itself within ~40 μm of tissue or a paper sheet.

17. (c) — gray is absorbed dose; sievert is weighted dose (risk).

18. (b) — Tc-99m: 140 keV γ, 6 h half-life, versatile chemistry — the workhorse of nuclear medicine.

19. (a) — the antineutrino (in β⁻) takes a variable share (Pauli's prophecy, confirmed 1956).

20. (d) — a thermal neutron tips U-235 into fission; the 2–3 emitted neutrons sustain the chain.

21. (b) — same Z, different N: same element, (nearly) same chemistry.

22. (d) — radius ∝ A^{1/3} ⇒ constant nuclear density, \sim 10^{17} kg m⁻³.

23. (c) — e^+e^- \to 2\gamma, each 511 keV, back-to-back: PET's coincidence signature.

24. (a) — λ is fixed by the nucleus; ordinary physical/chemical means do not touch it.

25. (c) — boron-10 and cadmium greedily capture neutrons, throttling the chain.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (c) — products sit higher on the BE/A curve; the gain in binding is paid out as energy.

2. (d) — positive "binding energy" would mean it falls apart for free: bound systems must mass less than their parts.

3. (a) — α's range is tens of μm in tissue: paper/dead skin stops them outside, but inhaled radon daughters deposit that dense ionization in lung tissue (weighting factor 20).

4. (b) — 1/8 = three halvings in 15 days: T_{1/2} = 5 days.

5. (d) — n \to p + e^- + \bar\nu_e creates the electron at the moment of decay; nuclei contain no electrons (d's caveat). Electron-cloud electrons (a) are unaffected apart from the changed Z.

6. (b) — criticality is neutron bookkeeping: production must at least balance escape + absorption, which needs enough fuel volume per surface.

7. (c) — slower decayer, fewer decays per second from the same stock.

8. (a) — in a day it is ~94 % gone: good pictures, minimal residual dose.

9. (b) — decay often lands the daughter on an upper rung of its own ladder; γ is the step down. ^{99m}Tc's "m" is exactly such a metastable rung.

10. (a) — two positive nuclei must be thrown together hard enough for the strong force (range ~fm) to grab: hence thermonuclear temperatures.

11. (d) — if every nucleon bound every other, BE would grow with the number of pairs (~A^2) and BE/A would keep rising with A; saturation (near-neighbour-only) flattens it, letting Coulomb's Z^2 drag win at large A.

12. (c) — while alive, intake replenishes C-14 as fast as it decays; death stops the exchange.

13. (a) — point source: intensity \propto 1/r^2 — the cheapest shielding is distance.

14. (d) — α: (90, 234); each β⁻: Z + 1 keeping A → (92, 234): back to uranium, a lighter isotope. (This is why decay chains meander.)

15. (b) — (1/2)^{10} = 1/1024 \approx 0.1\%: the ten-half-life rule of hospital waste stores.

  1. State the law of radioactive decay and derive the relation between half-life, mean life and decay constant. Explain the types of radiation and solve numericals. [10]
  2. Define mass defect and binding energy, and explain nuclear fission and fusion with numericals. [10]

Model answer D1: radioactive decay (10 marks)

Introduction. Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from unstable nuclei (Becquerel, 1896). It is a random, statistical process unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.

Radiations.

Property Alpha Beta Gamma
Nature helium nucleus {}^4_2\text{He} electron (or positron) photon
Charge +2e -e 0
Penetration paper stops it few mm of aluminium thick lead
Ionising power highest medium lowest
Effect on the nucleus A decreases by 4, Z by 2 Z changes by 1, A same no change in A, Z

Law of decay. The rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei: \dfrac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N, so N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}, where \lambda is the decay constant.

  1. Half-life T_{1/2}: time for half the nuclei to decay, T_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln2}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}.
  2. Mean life \tau = \dfrac1\lambda = 1.44\,T_{1/2}.
  3. Activity A = \lambda N = A_0e^{-\lambda t}, in becquerel (1\ \text{Bq} = 1\ \text{decay per second}; 1\ \text{Ci} = 3.7\times10^{10}\ \text{Bq}).
  4. After n half-lives, N = N_0/2^n.

Uses. Carbon dating, medical tracers and cancer therapy (cobalt-60), sterilisation of food, smoke detectors and thickness gauges.

Numerical. A sample of 64\ \text{g} with T_{1/2} = 8 days leaves 64/2^3 = 8\ \text{g} after 24 days. In carbon dating, a wooden relic that has 25\% of the original {}^{14}\text{C} is 2\times5730 = 11\,460 years old.

For T_{1/2} = 5\ \text{days}, \lambda = 0.693/5 = 0.139\ \text{day}^{-1} and the mean life is 7.2 days.

Conclusion. Decay is exponential. After each half-life the activity halves, whatever the starting amount.

Model answer D2: binding energy, fission and fusion (10 marks)

Introduction. The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its nucleons. This difference is the mass defect \Delta m = Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n - M.

By Einstein's relation E = mc^2, the binding energy is E_b = \Delta m\times931.5\ \text{MeV} (for \Delta m in u).

Binding energy curve. E_b/A rises steeply to about 8.8\ \text{MeV} at {}^{56}\text{Fe} (the most stable) and then falls slowly to 7.6\ \text{MeV} for uranium. Light nuclei can release energy by fusion, and heavy nuclei by fission.

Feature Fission Fusion
Process heavy nucleus splits light nuclei join
Example {}^{235}\text{U} + n \to {}^{141}\text{Ba} + {}^{92}\text{Kr} + 3n \text{D} + \text{T} \to {}^4\text{He} + n
Energy per reaction about 200\ \text{MeV} 17.6\ \text{MeV}
Energy per kilogram high even higher
Conditions slow neutrons 10^7 to 10^8\ \text{K}
Use reactors, bombs the sun, hydrogen bomb
Waste radioactive little

Nuclear reactor. The fuel is enriched uranium, the moderator (heavy water or graphite) slows neutrons, control rods (cadmium, boron) absorb neutrons to keep the multiplication factor k = 1, and the coolant removes heat.

In a bomb, k > 1 and the chain reaction is uncontrolled.

Numerical. For {}^4_2\text{He}: \Delta m = 2(1.007825) + 2(1.008665) - 4.002603 = 0.029377\ \text{u}, so E_b = 0.029377\times931.5 = 27.4\ \text{MeV} and E_b/A = 6.84\ \text{MeV} per nucleon.

Fission of 1\ \text{kg} of {}^{235}\text{U} involves \dfrac{1000}{235}\times6.02\times10^{23} = 2.56\times10^{24} nuclei, giving 2.56\times10^{24}\times200\ \text{MeV} = 8.2\times10^{13}\ \text{J}, which equals about 2.3\times10^{7}\ \text{kWh}.

Conclusion. Energy is released when nuclei move toward the peak of the binding energy curve, by fission for heavy nuclei and by fusion for light ones.
